Remote libSQL and Turso

Source: vignettes/libsql.Rmd
libsql.Rmd

libSQL is based on SQLite and can run as a remote database server. Turso provides hosted databases with compatible SQL APIs. With shinyOAuthDB, your Shiny app can run SQLite SQL on these servers using the signed-in visitor’s access token.

oauth_db_libsql_api() sends queries over HTTPS and returns data frames, without a database driver. The server must accept tokens from your sign-in provider. Self-hosted libSQL and Turso Cloud have different requirements, explained after the example.

Try self-hosted libSQL locally

Start Docker and run:

shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_demo("libsql")

The demo starts self-hosted libSQL, Keycloak sign-in and a Shiny app. Alice and Bob can read the shared sample table; Try a write checks that the database refuses writes. See Getting started for passwords and cleanup.

Use oauth_db_demo("libsql", action = "files") to inspect or change the configuration. The demo uses self-hosted libSQL; Turso Cloud needs the separate token setup described below.

Before running the app

Your server must accept visitor access tokens from your provider. Self-hosted libSQL and Turso Cloud use different token formats; check the requirements below with your administrator before reusing an existing login.

Setting Where to get it
OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_URL The database’s HTTPS URL, from Turso’s database details or your server administrator
OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_ISSUER The provider configured to issue compatible database tokens
Client ID and secret Your OAuth app registration
OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_AUDIENCE The provider’s API audience, if required; leave empty for self-hosted libSQL

Register http://localhost:8100 as the redirect URI. The app’s sqlite.read scope is an example your provider must define or replace. Save the settings in .Renviron and restart R:

OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret
OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_ISSUER=https://your-provider.example.org/
OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_URL=libsql://your-database-your-org.turso.io
OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_AUDIENCE=your-provider-api-audience

A complete app

Replace the table name and scopes for your database. The provider’s token configuration must satisfy the requirements above before running the app.

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

audience <- Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_AUDIENCE")
provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_ISSUER"),
  extra_auth_params = if (nzchar(audience)) {
    list(audience = audience)
  } else {
    list()
  }
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "sqlite.read")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  libsql <- oauth_db_libsql_api(
    auth$connection,
    url = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_URL"),
    required_scopes = "sqlite.read"
  )
  output$rows <- renderTable({
    libsql$query(
      "SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE country = :country LIMIT 20",
      parameters = list(country = "NL")
    )
  })
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*"),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at http://localhost:8100
# (viewers in RStudio/Positron/etc. cannot perform necessary redirects)

Run source("example.R"). The app waits for sign-in before sending SQL and clears the output on sign-out. Request offline_access too if your provider requires it to renew tokens.

Parameters and result types

Use an unnamed list for positional ? parameters, or a named list for named parameters. The client sends values separately from SQL:

libsql$query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE country = ?", list("NL"))
libsql$execute(
  "INSERT INTO events(value) VALUES (:value)",
  list(value = "signed in")
)
libsql$query("SELECT ? AS exact_integer", list(I("9223372036854775807")))
libsql$query("SELECT ? AS bytes, ? AS missing", list(as.raw(c(0, 255)), NULL))

SQLite integers return as strings to preserve all 64 bits. Floating-point values stay numeric; blobs and columns with mixed types use list columns. Format dates and timestamps as strings in the format your database uses. See ?oauth_db_libsql_api for conversions and statement metadata.

Request lifetime

Each call runs one statement in its own HTTPS request. Calls don’t share transactions or temporary tables; separate BEGIN and COMMIT calls can’t form a transaction. Use a database client with transaction support when your app needs that behavior.

The helper gets a current token for each call and discards results after sign-out or account changes. SQL requests don’t retry automatically. After an ambiguous write failure, check the database before resubmitting; a statement can finish even after the local app stops waiting.

Configure a compatible token issuer

Self-hosted libSQL

The self-hosted demo uses libSQL 0.24.33. Configure its Ed25519 public signing key with SQLD_AUTH_JWT_KEY_FILE or SQLD_AUTH_JWT_KEY, following the server’s authentication instructions.

Issue the database namespace in id, permissions in a ("ro" for read-only or "rw" for read/write), and an exp expiry. Set these explicitly: the tested server permits missing expiry and defaults missing permissions to write access. Its newer p format is another option; see the server token format.

This server verifies a configured signing key rather than discovering an OIDC provider. It rejects an aud claim in this configuration. Use a dedicated key and restrict token issuance to the intended database and users. A provider that can’t issue this format needs a separate gateway or token exchange; the R helper doesn’t create or exchange database tokens.

Expose the server through HTTPS. Use ca_bundle for a private certificate authority.

Turso Cloud external providers

Follow Turso’s external authentication setup for a supported provider such as Clerk or Auth0. Register the provider’s public signing-key endpoint and generate a database-specific JWT claims template with the Turso CLI. Restrict it to the database and operations the app needs, then configure your provider to issue those claims.

Pass that provider-issued access token through shinyOAuth to the database. A Turso management token or shared database token doesn’t carry the visitor’s own permissions.
